brief: Ahead of Thursday's Trump-Xi summit, JPMorgan, Deutsche Bank, TD Cowen and Raymond James agree no grand deal will emerge, only sustained but managed tension. The Busan trade truce, which paused tariffs and rare-earth export controls, expires November 10; every bank expects an extension, but the US reportedly wants about six months while China wants it to run through the end of Trump's term, so the length of the extension is the number that matters for markets. A '30 for 30' Board of Trade covering roughly $30 billion of goods per side is the likely headline deliverable, but legacy Section 301 tariffs stay in place and none of it moves the $202.7 billion 2025 goods deficit. JPMorgan sees the clearest upside in Iran: rerouted Hormuz flows have driven Brent to $130.80 and diesel above $6, and a deal converting Chinese leverage over Tehran into de-escalation could ease that risk. On Taiwan and AI, expectations are for rhetoric, not policy change. The bigger risk banks flag is after November 4, when the midterms end and Washington has more room to escalate: delisting, a VIE ban, or an investment ban.
